title: Docker Security
subtitle: Hardening containers, images and the daemon
description: Containers share the host kernel. Security is a set of layered controls: least privilege, minimal images, secret hygiene, provenance and daemon hardening.
outcomes: Apply non-root, capability, seccomp and filesystem controls
Manage secrets without baking them into images
Harden the Docker daemon and supply chain

lessons.title: The container security model
lessons.summary: What isolation gives you, what it does not, and the controls that actually reduce risk.
objectives: Name the default privileges of a container

sections.title: Shared kernel, shared risk
sections.body:
A container is a process on the host kernel with namespaces and cgroups. A kernel vulnerability or a misconfigured privileged container can compromise the host. Docker’s defaults are reasonable but not a security boundary on their own.

The highest-leverage controls are: run as non-root, drop unnecessary capabilities, use a read-only root filesystem, apply a seccomp profile, and never mount the Docker socket into an application container.

sections.code:
docker run -d --name hardened \
  --user 10001:10001 \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --security-opt seccomp=/etc/docker/seccomp.json \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --memory 256m --pids-limit 128 \
  nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged:1.27-alpine
sections.note: The unprivileged nginx image listens on 8080 and runs without root. Pair read-only with tmpfs for paths the app must write.

sections.title: Never mount docker.sock into an app
sections.body: It is a root-equivalent API. A compromised web app becomes a host compromise. Use a narrowly scoped proxy or a separate deployment mechanism.

exercises.title: Harden nginx
exercises.prompt: Run unprivileged nginx with a read-only root and tmpfs for /tmp.

exercises.title: Check capabilities
exercises.prompt: Inspect a container and list its capabilities.

questions.question: What is the strongest reason not to run as root?
options: A container escape or app compromise gains fewer host privileges

questions.question: What does --read-only do?
questions.explain: Writable paths must be explicitly mounted.

questions.question: Why is docker.sock dangerous in a container?
options: It grants control of the Docker daemon
questions.explain: The daemon can start privileged containers and mount host paths.

lessons.title: Secrets management
lessons.summary: Keep credentials out of images, environment variables and logs.
objectives: Use BuildKit secrets and Compose secrets

sections.title: Where secrets leak
sections.body: Secrets leak through image layers, build args, environment variables, logs, crash dumps, shell history, CI output, and world-readable files. Deleting a secret in a later Dockerfile layer does not remove it from the earlier layer.

head: Mechanism
Safe for secrets?
Why
rows: Mounted at runtime, not in image

sections.code:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:20-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

sections.title: Rotation is part of secret management
sections.body: A secret that cannot be rotated is an incident waiting to happen. Prefer short-lived tokens and automate rotation.

exercises.title: Build secret
exercises.prompt: Write a RUN that uses a secret named pip_conf.

exercises.title: Audit an image
exercises.prompt: Find environment variables that look sensitive.
exercises.expected: docker image inspect IMAGE --format "{{json .Config.Env}}" and grep for TOKEN/PASSWORD/KEY.

questions.question: Which build mechanism is safe for secrets?
questions.explain: Secret mounts are not stored in layers.

questions.question: Why is deleting a secret in a later layer insufficient?
options: The earlier layer still contains it
questions.explain: Image layers are additive; history remains.

questions.question: What is the best long-term secret strategy?
options: A secret manager with rotation and least privilege
questions.explain: Central management and rotation reduce exposure.

lessons.title: Scanning, SBOMs and signing
lessons.summary: Know what is in an image, where it came from, and whether it has been tampered with.

sections.title: Three questions
sections.body:
**What is inside?** A software bill of materials (SBOM) lists packages and versions. **Is it vulnerable?** A scanner maps packages to advisories. **Is it the image I built?** A signature and provenance attestation answer that.

Docker Scout, Trivy, Grype and registry-native scanners cover the first two. Sigstore/cosign and Docker’s attestations cover provenance. Pin base images and rebuild regularly; scanners only help if you act on results.

sections.code:
# Docker Scout (when available)
docker scout cves registry.example.com/acme/api:1.4
docker scout sbom registry.example.com/acme/api:1.4

# BuildKit provenance and SBOM attestations
docker buildx build \
  --provenance=true --sbom=true \
  -t registry.example.com/acme/api:1.4 --push .

# cosign verification (if signatures are used)
cosign verify registry.example.com/acme/api:1.4 \
  --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/acme/.*' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
sections.note: Scanners and cosign are separate tools; OpsDeck does not install them for you.

sections.title: SBOMs are not a security feature by themselves
sections.body: They are inventory. Pair them with continuous scanning and a rebuild policy.

exercises.title: Generate attestations
exercises.prompt: Build with provenance and SBOM and push.

exercises.title: Scan
exercises.prompt: Run a vulnerability scan on an image you use.
exercises.expected: docker scout cves IMAGE or trivy image IMAGE.

questions.question: What does an SBOM contain?
options: A list of components and versions
questions.explain: It is a software bill of materials.

questions.question: What does cosign verify prove?
options: The signature matches a trusted identity

questions.question: Why rebuild images regularly?
options: To pick up base image and dependency security fixes
questions.explain: New vulnerabilities are disclosed after an image is built.

lessons.title: Daemon and host hardening
lessons.summary: The engine is the real privileged component. Protect its socket, configuration and update path.
objectives: Harden the Docker socket and remote access
Configure daemon logging and user namespaces

sections.title: The daemon is root
sections.body: Anyone with socket access can mount the host filesystem and start a privileged container. Restrict the socket with filesystem permissions, avoid exposing TCP without mutual TLS, and never give application containers the socket. Rootless mode runs the daemon as a normal user, reducing the impact of a daemon compromise at the cost of some networking and storage features.

sections.note: daemon.json lives at /etc/docker/daemon.json on Linux. Validate with dockerd --validate --config-file and restart deliberately.

sections.code:
# Check socket ownership
ls -l /var/run/docker.sock

# Rootless mode
dockerd-rootless-setuptool.sh install
systemctl --user status docker

# Audit daemon config
docker info --format '{{json .SecurityOptions}}'

sections.title: Remote TCP without TLS is host takeover
sections.body: Port 2375 has no authentication. Use `dockerd --tlsverify` with mutual TLS, or SSH contexts, and firewall the port.

exercises.title: Audit socket
exercises.prompt: Check the permissions and group of docker.sock.

questions.question: What is the safest way to give a CI job access to Docker?
options: Use a dedicated remote engine with scoped credentials
questions.explain: Isolate the engine and scope credentials.

questions.question: What does rootless mode change?
options: Runs the daemon as a non-root user

questions.question: Why set log rotation?
options: To stop logs filling the host disk
